description: Functions for solving equations and inequalities exactly and numerically, for quantifier elimination over the reals, for constrained and unconstrained optimization including the modern convex optimization solvers, and for fitting models and interpolating data. Exact solvers work over specified domains (Reals, Integers, Complexes) while the N-prefixed solvers work numerically from a starting point or over a search region.

tools.name: Solve
tools.description: Solves equations and systems of equations symbolically, returning a list of replacement rules, one list per solution. A third argument names variables to eliminate, and the Domain specification (Reals, Integers, Complexes) restricts the solution set. Solve is designed for generically finite solution sets; it may issue Solve::svars and omit degenerate cases, for which Reduce is the complete alternative.
tools.usage:
Solve[eqns, vars]
Solve[eqns, vars, dom]
Solve[eqns, vars, elims]
Solve[eqns && ineqs, vars, Reals]

parameters.name: eqns
parameters.description: Equation or list/And of equations using == (not =); inequalities are allowed when a domain is given.

parameters.name: dom
parameters.description: Reals, Integers, Complexes, Rationals or Primes, restricting the solution domain.

tools.example:
Solve[x^2 == 4, x]
Solve[{x + y == 3, x - y == 1}, {x, y}]
Solve[x^2 + y^2 == 1 && x > 0, {x, y}, Reals]
x /. Solve[a x^2 + b x + c == 0, x]
Solve[x^2 + 3 x + 2 == 0, x, Integers]
tools.notes: Use == for equations; a single = performs an assignment. SolveValues returns the values directly instead of rules, avoiding the /. step.

tools.name: SolveValues
tools.description: Solves equations and returns the list of solution values directly rather than replacement rules, so no ReplaceAll step is needed. For a single variable it returns a flat list of values; for several variables it returns a list of value tuples. It accepts the same equations, domains and options as Solve.
tools.usage:
SolveValues[eqns, vars]
SolveValues[eqns, vars, dom]
tools.example:
SolveValues[x^2 == 4, x]
SolveValues[{x + y == 3, x y == 2}, {x, y}]
SolveValues[x^3 - 1 == 0, x, Reals]
Max[SolveValues[x^2 - 5 x + 6 == 0, x]]
tools.notes: Introduced in Wolfram Language 13.0; in earlier versions write x /. Solve[...]. NSolveValues and DSolveValue follow the same pattern.

tools.name: NSolve
tools.description: Finds all numerical solutions of a polynomial equation or system, returning rules just like Solve. Unlike FindRoot it needs no starting point and it finds every root, including complex ones, up to the requested working precision. For non-polynomial equations it can still work over a bounded region when a domain and constraints are supplied.
tools.usage:
NSolve[eqns, vars]
NSolve[eqns, vars, dom]
NSolve[eqns, vars, WorkingPrecision -> p]
tools.example:
NSolve[x^5 - 3 x + 1 == 0, x]
NSolve[x^3 == 2, x, Reals]
NSolve[{x^2 + y^2 == 4, y == x^2}, {x, y}]
NSolve[x^4 + 1 == 0, x, WorkingPrecision -> 30]
tools.notes: NSolve is the right choice for polynomials of moderate degree; for large systems or transcendental equations use FindRoot with a good starting value.

tools.name: FindRoot
tools.description: Finds a numerical root of an equation or system starting from a given initial value, using Newton's method by default or the secant, Brent or damped Newton methods. It finds one root near the starting point rather than all roots, so a good initial guess matters. Supplying two starting values switches to a bracketing/secant method that needs no derivative.
tools.usage:
FindRoot[f, {x, x0}]
FindRoot[lhs == rhs, {x, x0}]
FindRoot[{eq1, eq2}, {{x, x0}, {y, y0}}]
FindRoot[f, {x, x0, xmin, xmax}]

parameters.name: WorkingPrecision
parameters.description: Internal precision; raise for high-accuracy roots.

parameters.name: Jacobian
parameters.description: Explicit Jacobian for systems, avoiding numerical differentiation.

tools.example:
FindRoot[Cos[x] == x, {x, 1}]
FindRoot[x^3 - 2, {x, 1, 2}]
FindRoot[{x^2 + y^2 == 4, x y == 1}, {{x, 1}, {y, 1}}]
FindRoot[Exp[x] == 3 x, {x, 0}, WorkingPrecision -> 30]
tools.notes: If the function is expensive or noisy, define it with the _?NumericQ pattern and supply bracketing values so a derivative-free method is used.

tools.name: Reduce
tools.description: Gives a complete description of the solution set of equations and inequalities, as a logical combination of simpler conditions rather than a list of rules. It never drops degenerate cases, so it reports exactly which parameter values give which solutions, and it performs real quantifier elimination via cylindrical algebraic decomposition. Domains Reals, Integers, Complexes and Booleans are all supported.
tools.usage:
Reduce[expr, vars]
Reduce[expr, vars, dom]
Reduce[ForAll[x, cond], params, Reals]
tools.example:
Reduce[a x == b, x]
Reduce[x^2 + y^2 < 1, {x, y}, Reals]
Reduce[x^2 - 3 x + 2 == 0 && x > 1, x]
Reduce[3 x + 5 y == 7, {x, y}, Integers]
Reduce[ForAll[x, x^2 + b x + 1 > 0], b, Reals]
tools.notes: Reduce output is a logical expression; convert it to rules with ToRules when a list of solutions is needed. It can be much slower than Solve because it is complete.

tools.name: FindInstance
tools.description: Finds one or more specific instances that satisfy a system of equations and inequalities over a given domain, without describing the whole solution set. It is the practical way to get a witness for a satisfiable system, including integer and Diophantine problems where Reduce would be far too slow. A count argument requests several distinct instances.
tools.usage:
FindInstance[expr, vars]
FindInstance[expr, vars, dom]
FindInstance[expr, vars, dom, n]
tools.example:
FindInstance[x^2 + y^2 == 25, {x, y}, Integers]
FindInstance[x > 0 && Sin[x] == 1/2, x, Reals]
FindInstance[a + b + c == 10 && a < b < c, {a, b, c}, Integers, 3]
FindInstance[x^2 < 2 && x > 1, x, Reals]
tools.notes: An empty result {} means the system is unsatisfiable over that domain, which is a useful proof of infeasibility.

tools.name: Root
tools.description: Represents an exact algebraic number as the k-th root of a polynomial, which is how Solve returns roots of degree five and higher that have no radical form. Root objects are exact: they can be compared, ordered, arbitrarily numericized with N, and simplified. Root[f, k] with a pure function argument specifies the defining polynomial directly.
tools.usage:
Root[poly, k]
Root[f, k]
N[Root[...], prec]
ToRadicals[root]
tools.example:
Solve[x^5 - x + 1 == 0, x]
r = Root[#^5 - # + 1 &, 1];
N[r, 40]
ToRadicals[Root[#^3 - 2 &, 1]]
MinimalPolynomial[Sqrt[2] + Sqrt[3], x]
tools.notes: Root objects are exact numbers, so arithmetic with them stays exact; use N only at the end. RootReduce puts an algebraic expression into canonical Root form.

tools.name: Roots
tools.description: Gives the roots of a polynomial equation as a logical Or of equations of the form x == value, rather than as replacement rules. It is the older interface underlying Solve for univariate polynomials and is occasionally convenient when the logical form is wanted. ToRules converts its output into rules.
tools.usage:
Roots[lhs == rhs, x]
ToRules[Roots[eqn, x]]
tools.example:
Roots[x^2 - 3 x + 2 == 0, x]
ToRules[Roots[x^3 == 1, x]]
Roots[x^2 + 1 == 0, x]
Roots[a x^2 + b x + c == 0, x]

tools.name: ToRules
tools.description: Converts the logical output of Roots or Reduce into the sequence of replacement-rule lists that Solve would return. Wrap it in {} to get an ordinary list of solutions. It is the bridge between the complete logical descriptions and the rule-based interface expected by the rest of the language.
tools.usage:
ToRules[expr]
{ToRules[Reduce[...]]}
tools.notes: ToRules only works on expressions that are disjunctions of equations; inequality-bearing Reduce output cannot be turned into rules.

tools.name: Resolve
tools.description: Eliminates quantifiers from a logical statement containing ForAll and Exists, returning an equivalent quantifier-free condition on the free variables. Over the reals it uses cylindrical algebraic decomposition, which is complete but potentially expensive. It is the tool for proving that a family of inequalities holds for all parameter values.
tools.usage:
Resolve[expr]
Resolve[expr, dom]
Resolve[ForAll[x, cond], Reals]
tools.example:
Resolve[Exists[x, x^2 + b x + 1 == 0], Reals]
Resolve[ForAll[x, x^2 + b x + 1 > 0], Reals]
Resolve[Exists[{x, y}, x + y == 1 && x y == 2], Reals]
tools.notes: Reduce with a quantified argument performs the same elimination and is usually the more convenient entry point.

tools.name: ForAll
tools.description: Represents the universal quantifier, with Exists as the existential counterpart, for use inside Reduce, Resolve, Refine and Simplify. ForAll[x, cond, expr] restricts the quantification to values of x satisfying cond. Together they let you state and mechanically decide statements about all or some values of a variable.
tools.usage:
ForAll[x, expr]
ForAll[x, cond, expr]
Exists[x, expr]
Exists[x, cond, expr]
tools.example:
Reduce[ForAll[x, x^2 + a >= 0], a, Reals]
Resolve[Exists[x, x > 0 && x^2 == 2], Reals]
Reduce[ForAll[x, 0 < x < 1, x^2 < x], Reals]
Simplify[ForAll[x, x^2 >= 0], x \[Element] Reals]
tools.notes: Quantifier elimination over the reals is decidable but doubly exponential in the number of variables, so keep the quantified variable count small.

tools.name: Minimize
tools.description: Finds the exact global minimum of an expression, subject to optional constraints, returning {minimumValue, {rulesForVariables}}. It works symbolically over Reals by default and also over Integers, and handles polynomial, linear and many other constrained problems exactly. For problems where no closed form exists, use NMinimize.
tools.usage:
Minimize[f, vars]
Minimize[{f, cons}, vars]
Minimize[{f, cons}, vars, dom]
tools.example:
Minimize[x^2 + 3 x + 2, x]
Minimize[{x + y, x^2 + y^2 == 1}, {x, y}]
Minimize[{x y, x + y == 10 && x > 0 && y > 0}, {x, y}]
Minimize[{x + 2 y, 3 x + y >= 7 && x >= 0 && y >= 0}, {x, y}, Integers]

tools.name: Maximize
tools.description: Finds the exact global maximum of an expression, subject to optional constraints, with the same interface and domains as Minimize. It returns {maximumValue, rules} and works symbolically, so parameters may remain in the answer. Use ArgMax when only the maximizing point is wanted.
tools.usage:
Maximize[f, vars]
Maximize[{f, cons}, vars]
Maximize[{f, cons}, vars, dom]
tools.example:
Maximize[-x^2 + 4 x, x]
Maximize[{x y, x + y == 10}, {x, y}]
Maximize[{Sin[x], 0 <= x <= Pi}, x]
Maximize[{3 x + 2 y, x + y <= 4 && x >= 0 && y >= 0}, {x, y}]

tools.name: NMinimize
tools.description: Finds a numerical global minimum of a function over a region, using global search methods rather than local descent. Methods include "NelderMead", "DifferentialEvolution", "SimulatedAnnealing" and "RandomSearch", which makes it suitable for multimodal and non-smooth objectives. Constraints may be equalities, inequalities or domain specifications including Integers.
tools.usage:
NMinimize[f, vars]
NMinimize[{f, cons}, vars]
NMinimize[{f, cons}, vars, Method -> m]

parameters.name: MaxIterations
parameters.description: Iteration budget for the global search.

tools.example:
NMinimize[x^4 - 3 x^2 + x, x]
NMinimize[{x^2 + y^2, x + y >= 1}, {x, y}]
NMinimize[{Sin[x] + Sin[2 x], 0 <= x <= 10}, x, Method -> "DifferentialEvolution"]
NMinimize[{cost[a, b], a \[Element] Integers && 0 <= a <= 10}, {a, b}]
tools.notes: NMinimize attempts a global minimum and is slower; FindMinimum converges quickly to a local minimum from a starting point.

tools.name: NMaximize
tools.description: Finds a numerical global maximum of a function subject to constraints, with the same methods and options as NMinimize. Use it for multimodal objectives where a local optimizer would get trapped. The result is {maximumValue, rules}.
tools.usage:
NMaximize[f, vars]
NMaximize[{f, cons}, vars]
tools.example:
NMaximize[-x^2 + 4 x, x]
NMaximize[{x y, x^2 + y^2 <= 1}, {x, y}]
NMaximize[{profit[q], 0 <= q <= 100}, q, Method -> "SimulatedAnnealing"]

tools.name: FindMinimum
tools.description: Finds a local numerical minimum starting from a given point, using quasi-Newton, conjugate gradient, Newton or Levenberg-Marquardt methods. It converges quickly for smooth problems but returns whichever local minimum is nearest the start. Gradient and Hessian can be supplied explicitly through options to speed convergence.
tools.usage:
FindMinimum[f, {x, x0}]
FindMinimum[f, {{x, x0}, {y, y0}}]
FindMinimum[{f, cons}, {{x, x0}}]

parameters.name: Gradient
parameters.description: Explicit gradient expression, avoiding finite differences.

tools.example:
FindMinimum[x^2 + 3 x, {x, 0}]
FindMinimum[Cos[x] + x^2/10, {x, 3}]
FindMinimum[(x - 1)^2 + (y - 2)^2, {{x, 0}, {y, 0}}]
FindMinimum[{x^2 + y^2, x + y == 1}, {{x, 0}, {y, 0}}]

tools.name: FindMaximum
tools.description: Finds a local numerical maximum starting from given initial values, the counterpart of FindMinimum with the same methods and options. It returns {value, rules}. Use NMaximize when the objective has several local maxima and the global one is required.
tools.usage:
FindMaximum[f, {x, x0}]
FindMaximum[{f, cons}, {{x, x0}, {y, y0}}]
tools.example:
FindMaximum[-x^2 + 4 x, {x, 0}]
FindMaximum[Sin[x], {x, 1}]
FindMaximum[{x y, x^2 + y^2 == 1}, {{x, 1}, {y, 0}}]

tools.name: ArgMin
tools.description: Gives the exact point at which an expression attains its global minimum, rather than the minimum value itself. Constraints and a domain are specified exactly as for Minimize. It is the cleaner form when you only care where the optimum is.
tools.usage:
ArgMin[f, vars]
ArgMin[{f, cons}, vars]
ArgMin[{f, cons}, vars, dom]
tools.example:
ArgMin[x^2 + 3 x + 2, x]
ArgMin[{x + y, x^2 + y^2 == 1}, {x, y}]
ArgMin[{x^2, x >= 1}, x]
ArgMin[{Norm[a . v - b], v}, v]

tools.name: ArgMax
tools.description: Gives the exact point at which an expression attains its global maximum, subject to any constraints and over a chosen domain. It is the maximizing counterpart of ArgMin and complements Maximize, which returns the value. Both accept symbolic parameters and return symbolic answers where possible.
tools.usage:
ArgMax[f, vars]
ArgMax[{f, cons}, vars]
ArgMax[{f, cons}, vars, dom]
tools.example:
ArgMax[-x^2 + 4 x, x]
ArgMax[{x y, x + y == 10 && x > 0}, {x, y}]
ArgMax[{Sin[x], 0 < x < 2 Pi}, x]
ArgMax[{n (10 - n), 0 <= n <= 10}, n, Integers]

tools.name: FindArgMin
tools.description: Finds numerically the point at which a function attains a local minimum, starting from given initial values. It is FindMinimum without the objective value, which is convenient when the location is what you need. FindArgMax is the maximizing counterpart, and both accept the same methods and constraint syntax.
tools.usage:
FindArgMin[f, {x, x0}]
FindArgMin[{f, cons}, {{x, x0}, {y, y0}}]
FindArgMax[f, {x, x0}]
tools.example:
FindArgMin[x^2 + 3 x, {x, 0}]
FindArgMin[(x - 2)^2 + (y + 1)^2, {{x, 0}, {y, 0}}]
FindArgMax[Sin[x] Exp[-x/10], {x, 1}]
FindArgMin[Norm[m . v - b], {v, Array[0. &, 3]}]

tools.name: LinearProgramming
tools.description: Solves a linear program in the classical matrix form, minimizing c.x subject to m.x >= b and x >= 0. The constraint directions can be individually specified by pairing each right-hand side with -1, 0 or 1, and variable bounds are given as a list of {lower, upper} pairs. It is the low-level interface; LinearOptimization offers a more readable symbolic form.
tools.usage:
LinearProgramming[c, m, b]
LinearProgramming[c, m, {{b1, s1}, {b2, s2}, ...}]
LinearProgramming[c, m, b, bounds]

parameters.name: c
parameters.description: Coefficient vector of the linear objective to minimize.

parameters.name: b
parameters.description: Right-hand sides, optionally paired with -1 (<=), 0 (==) or 1 (>=).

tools.example:
LinearProgramming[{1, 1}, {{1, 2}, {3, 1}}, {3, 5}]
LinearProgramming[{-2, -3}, {{1, 1}, {2, 1}}, {{4, -1}, {6, -1}}]
LinearProgramming[c, m, b, Integers]
tools.notes: With exact rational input it gives exact answers using the simplex method; with machine numbers it uses fast floating-point solvers.

tools.name: LinearOptimization
tools.description: Solves linear optimization problems stated either symbolically with constraints or in matrix form, returning optimal variable values, the optimal value, or dual and sensitivity information. It supports integer and mixed-integer variables through a domain specification and reports certificates of infeasibility or unboundedness. It is the modern replacement for LinearProgramming in most code.
tools.usage:
LinearOptimization[f, cons, vars]
LinearOptimization[c, {m, b}]
LinearOptimization[f, cons, vars, "PrimalMinimizer"]
LinearOptimization[f, cons, vars \[Element] Integers]
tools.example:
LinearOptimization[x + y, {x + 2 y >= 3, 3 x + y >= 5, x >= 0, y >= 0}, {x, y}]
LinearOptimization[-2 x - 3 y, {x + y <= 4, x >= 0, y >= 0}, {x, y}, "PrimalMinimizerRules"]
LinearOptimization[c, {m, b}]
LinearOptimization[x + y, {2 x + y >= 3, x >= 0, y >= 0}, {x, y} \[Element] Integers]
tools.notes: Ask for "DualMaximizer" or "ConstraintSensitivity" as the property argument to get shadow prices for sensitivity analysis.

tools.name: QuadraticOptimization
tools.description: Minimizes a convex quadratic objective subject to linear constraints, stated symbolically or as matrices. It is the solver behind portfolio optimization, least squares with constraints and model predictive control. Integer variables and property requests such as dual values are supported in the same way as LinearOptimization.
tools.usage:
QuadraticOptimization[f, cons, vars]
QuadraticOptimization[{q, c}, {m, b}]
QuadraticOptimization[f, cons, vars, props]
tools.example:
QuadraticOptimization[x^2 + y^2, {x + y >= 1}, {x, y}]
QuadraticOptimization[{{{2, 0}, {0, 2}}, {0, 0}}, {{{1, 1}}, {1}}]
QuadraticOptimization[Norm[a . x - b]^2, {x >= 0}, x]
tools.notes: The quadratic term must be positive semidefinite for the problem to be convex; otherwise use NMinimize or ConvexOptimization with a reformulation.

tools.name: SecondOrderConeOptimization
tools.description: Solves optimization problems with a linear objective and second-order (Lorentz) cone constraints of the form Norm[a.x + b] <= c.x + d. Many robust optimization, facility location and norm-minimization problems are naturally second-order cone programs. Constraints may be written symbolically with Norm or supplied as explicit cone data.
tools.usage:
SecondOrderConeOptimization[f, cons, vars]
SecondOrderConeOptimization[c, {{a1, b1, al1, be1}, ...}]
tools.example:
SecondOrderConeOptimization[x + y, {Sqrt[x^2 + y^2] <= 1}, {x, y}]
SecondOrderConeOptimization[-x, {Norm[{x, y}] <= 2, y >= 1}, {x, y}]

tools.name: SemidefiniteOptimization
tools.description: Solves semidefinite programs: minimize a linear objective subject to linear matrix inequality constraints requiring a matrix to be positive semidefinite. These appear in control theory (Lyapunov and LMI conditions), relaxations of combinatorial problems and moment problems. Constraints are written with VectorGreaterEqual over the semidefinite cone or as explicit matrix data.
tools.usage:
SemidefiniteOptimization[f, cons, vars]
SemidefiniteOptimization[c, {a0, a1, ...}]
tools.example:
SemidefiniteOptimization[x, {VectorGreaterEqual[{{{1, x}, {x, 1}}, 0}, {"SemidefiniteCone", 2}]}, x]
SemidefiniteOptimization[-y, {VectorGreaterEqual[{{{1, y}, {y, 4}}, 0}, {"SemidefiniteCone", 2}]}, y]
tools.notes: Semidefinite programs are solved by interior-point methods in machine precision; check the returned objective against the constraint residuals for very ill-conditioned problems.

tools.name: ConicOptimization
tools.description: Solves optimization problems with a linear objective and constraints drawn from any mixture of the supported cones: nonnegative, second-order, semidefinite, exponential and power cones. It is the unifying interface beneath the specialized conic solvers. Problems are specified symbolically or with explicit cone data, and duals are available as properties.
tools.usage:
ConicOptimization[f, cons, vars]
ConicOptimization[c, {a, b}, cone]
tools.example:
ConicOptimization[x + y, {Norm[{x, y}] <= 1, x >= 0}, {x, y}]
ConicOptimization[-x, {Exp[x] <= y, y <= 3}, {x, y}]

tools.name: ConvexOptimization
tools.description: Solves general convex optimization problems written in natural symbolic form, automatically recognizing convexity and converting the problem to the appropriate conic form. It accepts objectives and constraints built from norms, logs, exponentials, quadratic forms and other convex atoms. Property requests give the minimizer, the optimal value, dual variables and sensitivity information.
tools.usage:
ConvexOptimization[f, cons, vars]
ConvexOptimization[f, cons, vars, props]
tools.example:
ConvexOptimization[Norm[{x, y}], {x + y >= 1}, {x, y}]
ConvexOptimization[-Log[x] - Log[y], {x + y <= 2, x > 0, y > 0}, {x, y}]
ConvexOptimization[Total[Abs[a . x - b]], {}, x]
ConvexOptimization[f, cons, vars, "DualMaximizer"]
tools.notes: If the problem is not recognized as convex an error is issued; ConvexFunctionQ and ConvexSetQ let you check convexity of an expression or region first.

tools.name: FindFit
tools.description: Finds the parameter values of an arbitrary model function that best fit data, by default in the least-squares sense. Starting values can be given with each parameter, which matters for nonlinear models. The NormFunction option switches to other criteria such as least absolute deviations.
tools.usage:
FindFit[data, expr, pars, vars]
FindFit[data, {expr, cons}, pars, vars]
FindFit[data, expr, {{p, p0}}, vars]
tools.example:
FindFit[{{1, 2}, {2, 4.1}, {3, 6.2}}, a x + b, {a, b}, x]
FindFit[data, a Exp[-b t], {{a, 1}, {b, 0.1}}, t]
FindFit[data, a x^2 + b x + c, {a, b, c}, x]
FindFit[data, model, pars, vars, NormFunction -> (Norm[#, 1] &)]
tools.notes: FindFit returns only the parameter rules; NonlinearModelFit returns a full model object with residuals, confidence intervals and diagnostics.

tools.name: LinearModelFit
tools.description: Fits a linear model (linear in its parameters) to data and returns a FittedModel object supporting dozens of diagnostic properties. Properties include "BestFit", "ParameterTable", "RSquared", "ANOVATable", "FitResiduals" and prediction intervals. The FittedModel can be evaluated like a function at new points.
tools.usage:
LinearModelFit[data, funs, vars]
LinearModelFit[{m, v}]
model["property"]
model[x]
tools.example:
lm = LinearModelFit[{{1, 2}, {2, 4.1}, {3, 5.9}}, x, x];
lm["BestFit"]
lm["RSquared"]
lm["ParameterTable"]
lm[4]
LinearModelFit[data, {1, x, x^2}, x]
tools.notes: The basis functions list may omit the constant term by giving IncludeConstantBasis -> False. Weights and a variance estimator function are available as options.

tools.name: NonlinearModelFit
tools.description: Fits a model that is nonlinear in its parameters, returning a FittedModel object with the same rich property interface as LinearModelFit. Starting values, parameter constraints and weights can all be specified, and the underlying optimization method is configurable. Use it when you need standard errors, confidence bands or residual diagnostics rather than just the parameter values.
tools.usage:
NonlinearModelFit[data, expr, pars, vars]
NonlinearModelFit[data, {expr, cons}, pars, vars]
model["property"]
tools.example:
nlm = NonlinearModelFit[data, a Exp[-b t], {{a, 1}, {b, 0.5}}, t];
nlm["BestFitParameters"]
nlm["ParameterConfidenceIntervalTable"]
nlm["FitResiduals"]
Show[ListPlot[data], Plot[nlm[t], {t, 0, 10}]]
tools.notes: Nonlinear fits are sensitive to starting values; plot the data first and choose starting parameters of the right order of magnitude.

tools.name: Fit
tools.description: Finds a least-squares fit of a linear combination of given basis functions to data, returning the fitted expression itself rather than a model object. It is the quickest way to get a polynomial or custom-basis fit when no diagnostics are needed. The basis list includes 1 explicitly when a constant term is wanted.
tools.usage: Fit[data, funs, vars]
tools.example:
Fit[{{1, 1}, {2, 4}, {3, 9}}, {1, x, x^2}, x]
Fit[data, {1, x}, x]
Fit[data, {1, Sin[x], Cos[x]}, x]
Fit[data3d, {1, x, y, x y}, {x, y}]
tools.notes: Fit gives no error estimates; use LinearModelFit when standard errors, R-squared or residual analysis are required.

tools.name: Interpolation
tools.description: Constructs an InterpolatingFunction that passes through given data points and can be evaluated, differentiated and integrated like an ordinary function. InterpolationOrder controls the polynomial degree used on each subinterval, with 3 the default and 1 giving piecewise linear interpolation. Data may be {y1, y2, ...} for unit-spaced points, {{x, y}, ...} pairs, or include derivative values.
tools.usage:
Interpolation[data]
Interpolation[data, InterpolationOrder -> n]
Interpolation[data, Method -> "Spline"]
func[x]
tools.notes: Evaluating outside the data range extrapolates and issues a warning; set the "ExtrapolationHandler" method option to control that behaviour. Use ListInterpolation for data on a regular multidimensional grid.

tools.name: ListInterpolation
tools.description: Builds an InterpolatingFunction from values given on a regular grid, with the coordinate ranges supplied separately. It is the multidimensional workhorse for interpolating gridded data such as images, simulation output or tabulated functions. InterpolationOrder and periodic boundary handling are available as options.
tools.usage:
ListInterpolation[array]
ListInterpolation[array, {{xmin, xmax}, {ymin, ymax}}]
ListInterpolation[array, {xgrid, ygrid}]

tools.name: InterpolatingPolynomial
tools.description: Gives the single polynomial of lowest degree that passes exactly through the supplied points, in Newton divided-difference form. Unlike Interpolation it returns a symbolic expression rather than a numerical function object. Derivative values can be specified at points to obtain Hermite interpolation.
tools.usage:
InterpolatingPolynomial[data, var]
InterpolatingPolynomial[{{x1, y1}, ...}, x]
tools.example:
InterpolatingPolynomial[{1, 4, 9, 16}, x]
Expand[InterpolatingPolynomial[{{0, 1}, {1, 3}, {2, 7}}, x]]
InterpolatingPolynomial[{{0, {1, 0}}, {1, {2, 1}}}, x]
tools.notes: High-degree interpolating polynomials oscillate badly between points (Runge phenomenon); prefer piecewise interpolation or splines for many data points.
